title: WHEA Corrected or Fatal Hardware Errors (Events 17–19)
exclusions: This rule reports Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger System events 17, 18, and 19: corrected hardware conditions for 17/19 and fatal hardware error 18. It does not claim that every WHEA provider event uses those semantics, and it excludes IDs 20, 46, 47 and other versions until their payload/severity is separately validated. It does not diagnose a failed component from numeric ErrorSource/ErrorType alone, predict a universal failure date, replace CPER/error-record analysis or vendor diagnostics, or prove hardware rather than firmware/driver/configuration causation. Systems that crash before forwarding, unsupported platforms, firmware-only logs, BMC/SEL, storage SMART, and collection gaps are outside scope. No ATT&CK or regulatory assurance is claimed.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `windows_whea_hardware_errors_17_19` saved search and ACL; schedule/job/alert history; every row with endpoint, event ID, severity label, ErrorSource/ErrorType, FRU/device/processor fields present, EventRecordID, SourceName, source, and source type; matching raw XML and WHEA error record/RawData; OEM diagnostics, firmware/driver/configuration and asset history; source-health evidence; dated controls; alert delivery; incident/work order; and bounded notification exception. This documentation-only review generated no hardware fault, WHEA event, Splunk job, alert, or diagnostic evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index and fixed window, replay three XML System fixtures with `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:System`, `SourceName=Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger`, `Computer=WIN-WHEA.example`, and distinct EventRecordIDs 40017-40019. Use EventCode 17 with ErrorSource `4` and PrimaryDeviceName `PCI\VEN_8086&DEV_1234`; EventCode 18 with ErrorSource `0`, ErrorType `9`, and ProcessorAPICID `2`; EventCode 19 with ErrorSource `0`, ErrorType `0`. Expect exactly three rows labeled respectively `corrected`, `fatal`, and `corrected`, preserving all raw diagnostic values. Documentation review checks logic only; no hardware fault or replay was performed.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for each: WHEA provider Event IDs 20, 46, and 47; Event 18 from another SourceName; Event 18 under Security source; Classic source type; malformed event code; empty endpoint; event at or after the exclusive latest boundary; and event outside the closed hour. Valid IDs 17 and 19 with blank optional ErrorType/FRU fields must still return corrected rows, and a valid 18 must remain fatal regardless of ErrorSource value.

dataSources: Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger Event IDs 17, 18, and 19 from each in-scope Windows endpoint's System channel, collected in XML with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1. The example uses local `index=wineventlog`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:System`, and provider field `SourceName=Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger`. Required system fields are `Computer`, `EventCode` or `EventID`, `EventRecordID`, `Level`, and `SourceName`; payloads vary by error record and can include `ErrorSource`, `ErrorType`, `FRUId`, `FRUText`, `PrimaryDeviceName`, `SecondaryDeviceName`, `ProcessorAPICID`, `RawData`, bus/device/function, status, and memory-location fields.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), version 10.0.1, for XML System-channel collection and field extraction. Splunkbase lists Splunk Enterprise 9.3 through current 10.x and Splunk Cloud support at review time. Test upgrades, especially across the documented 5.0.0 breaking-change boundary. OEM/BMC diagnostic tools are corroborating systems, not Splunkbase dependencies.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:System" SourceName="Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger" (EventCode=17 OR EventCode=18 OR EventCode=19) earliest=-70m@m latest=-10m@m
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), endpoint=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,Computer,host))), error_source=trim(ErrorSource), error_type=trim(ErrorType), hardware_component=trim(coalesce(Component,PrimaryDeviceName,FRUText))
| where event_code IN (17,18,19) AND len(endpoint)>0
| eval severity=case(event_code=18,"fatal",event_code IN (17,19),"corrected"), detection="Windows Hardware Error Architecture event observed"
| table _time endpoint event_code severity hardware_component error_source error_type FRUId FRUText PrimaryDeviceName SecondaryDeviceName ProcessorAPICID Bus Device Function Segment CorrectableErrorStatus UncorrectableErrorStatus Status RawData Level EventRecordID detection SourceName source sourcetype
| sort 0 -_time endpoint event_code EventRecordID
description: Reports one row for every collected WHEA-Logger System Event 17, 18, or 19 in the delayed closed hour, at hardware-error-event grain. It labels 17/19 as corrected and 18 as fatal while preserving endpoint, provider, available component/error-record fields, raw data, event level, and record identity.
value: Corrected hardware errors can reveal unstable PCIe, processor, memory, firmware, power, cooling, or board conditions before users report failures; fatal events require urgent incident and diagnostic review. Fleet-wide evidence helps operations correlate recurrence, protect workloads, dispatch the correct vendor team, and avoid replacing parts based on a single ambiguous message.
implementation: Collect the System channel in XML from every in-scope Windows endpoint with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows 10.0.1 and verify provider/payload fields across hardware models. Save `windows_whea_hardware_errors_17_19`, run hourly over `-70m@m` to `-10m@m`, and create one result per event. Route Event 18 urgently; trend 17/19 in a companion analytic using hardware/model-specific baselines rather than the unsupported universal `>10/hour` threshold removed from this UC.
visualization: On a hardware-reliability dashboard, put endpoint System-source freshness and hardware/firmware inventory coverage first. Add fatal and corrected counts, affected endpoints, trends by event ID/provider/error source/device, recurrence per asset, and a table with component, FRU/device identifiers, ErrorSource/ErrorType, event level, EventRecordID, firmware/driver versions, owner, work order, and disposition. Drill down to raw XML/RawData, nearby bugcheck/reboot events, BMC/SEL/OEM diagnostics, temperature/power telemetry, recent BIOS/driver/configuration changes, and workload impact.
schema: Native Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger System XML and WHEA/CPER error-record fields; no semantically equivalent Splunk CIM dataset is claimed
dataModelAcceleration: No `cimSpl` is supplied. The Windows add-on has historical model mappings for some event IDs, but a generic Updates, Event Signatures, Change, or Performance dataset is not a lossless hardware-error contract and may omit SourceName, EventRecordID, variable CPER fields, and RawData. A local summary can support trends only after model-specific field/row parity and acceleration freshness tests against raw XML.

knownFalsePositives:
A WHEA row represents a real condition reported through Windows. “False positive” means the event is expected, transient, duplicated, or not a physical part failure—not that the provider invented it.

1. **Known PCIe Advanced Error Reporting corrected-error storm** — Event 17 can recur for a particular root port/device because of firmware, chipset driver, link power management, cabling, or device behavior without user-visible failure. Match exact hardware ID, slot/bus/device/function, BIOS/driver version, OEM case/advisory, diagnostic results, and bounded risk acceptance. Never suppress all Event 17 fleet-wide.

2. **Approved BIOS/UEFI, chipset, driver, or firmware maintenance** — Restart and link retraining around an update may produce corrected events. Correlate package/version, signed deployment job, endpoint/model ring, reboot, UTC window, and post-change recurrence. Event 18 or continued errors after the window remain urgent.

3. **Hardware qualification, burn-in, stress, or fault-injection test** — Lab tools can intentionally expose marginal processor, memory, PCIe, thermal, or power behavior. Match test plan, asset/lab tag, operator, exact test interval, expected event IDs, sensors, and pass/fail criteria. Preserve results as qualification evidence.

4. **Overclocking, undervolting, power-policy, or thermal tuning** — An approved engineering experiment can cause corrected or fatal machine checks. Verify BIOS profile, owner, asset class, temperatures/voltages, test approval, and restoration to supported settings. Production systems should not receive broad exceptions for unsupported tuning.

5. **Hot-plug, docking, PCIe device reset, virtualization, or pass-through transition** — Supported device lifecycle operations may create transient corrected errors. Confirm hardware/model capability, hypervisor or docking action, device identity, maintenance/job record, and no recurrence or workload impact. A fatal event is not dismissed solely because hot-plug occurred.

6. **WEF plus direct-forwarder duplicate** — The same Computer/EventRecordID/provider can arrive twice. Confirm raw XML, route, `_indextime`, collector, and original endpoint. Repair collection topology; do not suppress the asset or provider.

**Safe suppression mechanism:** keep raw events and base results. In a notification wrapper, use a governed `windows_whea_notification_exceptions` lookup keyed on endpoint/asset ID, event code/severity, exact hardware model and device/FRU identifiers, ErrorSource/ErrorType where stable, approved firmware/driver/BIOS version, `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, owner, vendor case, and work order. Suppress only corrected-event notification for exact bounded matches; never blanket-suppress Event 18, all WHEA, a vendor, or an open-ended endpoint. Trend suppressed events and revoke the exception if rate, severity, device, or impact changes.
mitreAttack: N/A (WHEA hardware-health events are operational signals, not an adversary technique)

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and scope

Assign Windows platform, server/workstation hardware, datacenter/field support, firmware/driver, Splunk collection, service owner, incident, and exception owners. Inventory endpoint model/serial, CPU/memory/PCIe topology, BIOS/BMC/firmware/drivers, power/cooling, virtualization/pass-through, warranty, workload criticality, and OEM diagnostic access. Install `Splunk_TA_windows` 10.0.1 and test exact Windows/forwarder/add-on/Splunk versions and representative hardware models.

WHEA logs hardware error records to System through provider `Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger`. Error payloads vary by source and Common Platform Error Record section. This UC deliberately scopes IDs 17, 18, and 19 only: 17/19 corrected and 18 fatal. One event creates one row; no count threshold applies. A separate trend may baseline corrected recurrence by exact model/device. The prior unsupported universal >10 per hour predictor was removed.

The collector reads System; the search role reads `index=wineventlog` and schedules alerts but cannot update firmware, reboot, alter BIOS, suppress events, or close work orders. Protect RawData and hardware inventory.

## Step 1 — Collect and validate System XML

Configure a governed modular input:

```ini
[WinEventLog://System]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
checkpointInterval = 5
```

Record actual start/checkpoint/filter/routing settings. Validate with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and **Settings > Data Inputs**. Confirm `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:System`, and `SourceName=Microsoft-Windows-WHEA-Logger` from the XML Provider Name. Compare Computer, EventCode/EventID, Level, EventRecordID, and every available EventData field to Event Viewer XML. Do not rely on the human-rendered message as the only evidence.

Build System-source health for every asset. A healthy endpoint can have zero WHEA events, so use forwarder/channel freshness and controlled telemetry. For WEF/WEC, preserve original Computer, provider, EventRecordID, payload/RawData and arrival latency, and prevent direct-plus-collector duplication. Consider crash/queue behavior: fatal systems may fail before forwarding, so add BMC and reboot/bugcheck companions.

## Step 2 — Save and understand the search

Save as `windows_whea_hardware_errors_17_19`; run hourly at minute 5. Embedded `earliest=-70m@m latest=-10m@m` defines one closed 60 minute event-time window delayed 10 minutes. Measure p99 `_indextime-_time` and move both bounds equally if needed.

The base clause requires exact index, XML System source, provider SourceName, and IDs 17-19. Evaluation normalizes numeric ID/endpoint and common optional fields. The `where` clause reasserts IDs and nonempty endpoint. Severity is based only on scoped event semantics, not Event Viewer Level or ErrorSource. The table preserves one event, diagnostic fields, RawData, and EventRecordID. Empty optional fields remain empty because CPER sections differ.

No CIM replacement is claimed. Trend summaries may aggregate after the base search by endpoint, event code, stable device/FRU, and hardware/firmware version, but must retain drilldown and prove row parity.

## Step 3 — Validate without damaging equipment

Replay the three synthetic XML fixtures in an isolated index at fixed times and assert exact severity, endpoint, fields, record IDs, source, and provider. Run every negative separately: excluded WHEA IDs, wrong provider/channel/type, malformed ID, null endpoint, earliest inclusion, latest exclusion, and outside window. Test blank optional payloads, long RawData, hexadecimal fields, and duplicate Computer/EventRecordID.

Do not induce processor, memory, power, thermal, or PCIe failures in production. In a vendor-supported hardware lab, use OEM diagnostics or a safe existing captured event corpus; if corrected-error injection is officially supported, obtain hardware-owner approval and rollback. Validate Event Viewer, Splunk, urgent Event 18 routing, dashboard, and work-order integration without unsafe overclocking, undervolting, heat, component removal, or power interruption.

Record asset/model, BIOS/BMC/firmware/driver versions, input, fixture hash/captured-event provenance, exact UTC bounds, expected/actual rows, search job, notification, diagnostics, and owner acceptance. Keep `status=draft` until source coverage, model payloads, boundaries, fatal routing, dashboards, runbook, and exception behavior are human accepted.

## Step 4 — Triage and respond

Verify raw XML/provider/event identity and whether the row is corrected or fatal. Identify hardware component from CPER fields and asset topology; numeric ErrorSource/ErrorType can be architecture-specific. Correlate recurrence, Event 17/19 history, Event 18, WHEA IDs outside this scope, bugcheck 1001, unexpected shutdown/reboot, thermal/power/sensor data, BMC SEL, storage/network/device logs, workload errors, and recent BIOS/firmware/driver/hardware/configuration changes.

For Event 18, engage incident and hardware support urgently, protect workload availability, collect dump/error record and BMC/OEM diagnostics, and follow tested failover/drain/shutdown procedures. For corrected events, assess rate/change from model baseline, component identity, impact, and vendor guidance; schedule diagnostics or replacement when evidence supports it. Do not automatically reboot, power off, evacuate a cluster, flash firmware, change voltage, disable PCIe power management, or replace CPU/RAM from one ambiguous event.

Track vendor case, work order, diagnostics, remediation, recurrence-free observation, and returned-part analysis. Keep suppressed corrected events visible in trends. Review exceptions after hardware, slot, firmware, BIOS, driver, power, or cooling changes.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot

- **No WHEA events:** verify the endpoint actually logged one in System, exact provider, XML input, filters, forwarding/queues, index routing, and search permissions.
- **SourceName is missing/different:** inspect raw Provider Name and add-on extraction; fix the collection contract or explicitly adapt and retest rather than searching generic System errors.
- **Error fields are null:** expected across different CPER sections; inspect EventData and RawData, add-on version, and XML parsing. Do not manufacture component names.
- **Corrected errors flood:** group by exact model/device/firmware, compare rate and impact, engage OEM, and use finite notification suppression while retaining data.
- **Fatal event arrived after reboot:** inspect clocks, forwarder queues, crash persistence, WEF delay, and BMC/bugcheck companions; adjust both time bounds if needed.
- **Duplicate rows:** compare Computer/SourceName/EventRecordID and repair WEF/direct topology.
- **CIM/dashboard count differs:** compare raw event bounds, provider filter, summary freshness, and field availability; raw XML remains authoritative.
grandmaExplanation: We show when Windows says the computer's physical parts reported a corrected problem or a fatal one. That helps the hardware team investigate the right machine quickly without guessing that every warning means a part must be replaced.
hardware: Windows Vista/Server 2008 or later systems using WHEA, subject to platform firmware and hardware support. Payload fields vary among processor machine checks, PCIe AER, memory and platform error records. Maintain asset model, slot/device, BIOS/BMC, firmware, driver, cooling, power, and warranty context. WEF/WEC must preserve original Computer, provider, EventRecordID, RawData, and event time and avoid duplicate direct collection.
